headline: The SMTP DATA-body smuggling check covers every non-canonical dot-terminator
summary:
`b.guardSmtpCommand.detectBodySmuggling`, which the MX and submission listeners run on every DATA chunk and BDAT body, refused a `.`-alone-line terminated by `
.
`, `
.
`, `
.
`, or `.`, but let three more slip through: `.
`, `
.`, and `
.`. The last is the `<CR><LF>.<CR>` shape Exim accepted in the CVE-2023-51766 disclosure, so a hostile sender could still terminate a message in a way a lenient downstream relay reads as end-of-data and smuggle a second message after it. The check now refuses any `.`-alone-line whose surrounding line endings are not both canonical CRLF, matched across chunk boundaries, while still passing a lone bare LF or CR that is not such a terminator so a binary BDAT body is not refused for its content.

items.title: SMTP DATA-body smuggling detection covers every non-canonical dot-terminator
items.body:
SMTP smuggling (CVE-2023-51764 / -51765 / -51766) terminates a message with a `.` on a line whose line endings are not the canonical `
.
`, so a downstream relay that accepts the non-canonical form as end-of-data resumes parsing the next bytes as a second, unauthorized message. `b.guardSmtpCommand.detectBodySmuggling`, run by `b.mail.server.mx` and `b.mail.server.submission` on every DATA chunk and BDAT body, enumerated only four of the seven shapes and missed `.
`, `
.`, and `
.` (the `<CR><LF>.<CR>` form named in the CVE-2023-51766 Exim disclosure). It now refuses a `.`-alone-line whenever the line ending before or after the dot is a bare LF or bare CR rather than a canonical CRLF, deciding the same verdict whether the terminator arrives whole or split across two DATA chunks. A lone bare LF or CR that does not form such a dot-terminator is still accepted, so a binary BDAT body is not refused for carrying those bytes.

items.title: `b.guardTemplate` documents that it does not screen Pug source-code lines
items.body: `b.guardTemplate` refuses delimited template markers, including Pug `#{...}` / `!{...}` interpolation. Its docblock now records the boundary of that screen: an indentation-based engine (Pug, HAML) also compiles a buffered `=` / `!=` line, an unbuffered `-` line, a control keyword, an attribute expression, and a mixin call as code, and that code is un-delimited and syntactically indistinguishable from ordinary prose (a domain, a Markdown link, an `x = y` assignment), so a marker scan cannot flag it without refusing that prose. Untrusted input must therefore never be compiled as a Pug or HAML template, whatever this guard reports.
